strengths: The problem is well motivated. Figure 1 provides a clear analytical example showing why both ignoring context and intervening on every controllable variable can prevent optimal performance.
Combining causal policy-scope reduction with contextual Bayesian optimisation offers a useful approach to continuous intervention problems beyond the discrete settings discussed in related work.

The experiments distinguish settings where baseline optima are attainable from settings where they are structurally unattainable. Using a common HEBO backend, 110 random seeds, uncertainty estimates, and analytically tractable environments strengthens the comparisons.
weaknesses: The main regret proof has unresolved probability arguments. Appendix A applies a single-GP confidence result to the globally optimal function, although its index is selected from the random GP draws; taking maximum smoothness constants does not establish simultaneous confidence across all m functions. Additionally, the stated schedule sums π_t to one, whereas the failure-probability calculation using log(π_t) requires summability of 1/π_t. Theorem 4.1 needs a corrected, complete proof.

Theorem 4.1 analyzes Algorithm 1, not the proposed CoCa-BO algorithm. In Algorithm 2, each outer-bandit arm has changing rewards because its HEBO policy is learning. Section 5.2's observation that rewards become stationary at optimality does not justify ordinary UCB during learning or control the bias from earlier poor policies. Finite, decreasing average-regret curves do not establish the general convergence and sublinear-regret claims. The theorem's applicability to the implemented HEBO-based CaBO variant also requires clarification.

The contribution is substantially an integration of existing POMPS theory, HEBO, and UCB. Moreover, multi-function BO can be represented as standard GP-UCB on a disjoint union of domains with a block-diagonal kernel, with the usual regret definition on that domain. The manuscript should explain what theoretical advance goes beyond this reduction instead of presenting the regret formulation as fundamentally different.

Definition 3.3 does not correctly handle equivalent or nested policy scopes. Adding an admissible context allows a policy to ignore that context, so the enlarged policy class cannot have a worse optimum. Consequently, strict superiority over every other MPS excludes reduced scopes such as those used in Appendix D. The required minimality or equivalence restriction must be specified before invoking POMPS completeness.

The evaluation does not isolate the proposed scope-selection mechanism. CoCa-BO has only one or two candidate scopes in the reported examples, and the PSA experiments have only one, so they cannot demonstrate improved selection. Comparisons against uniform allocation and acquisition-based selection over the same POMPSes are missing. The small collection of constructed SCMs, including a larger graph dominated by redundant variables, provides limited evidence for broad effectiveness or scalability; scope-enumeration runtime is not reported.

Benchmark specifications contain consequential inconsistencies. Appendix B.2's printed PSA equation omits Cancer, so its subsequent square completion and claimed zero optimum do not follow. Appendix E drops the 0.1 coefficients multiplying both noise terms in Appendix C.1, overstating their variance contribution by a factor of 100; a stated ε_Y standard deviation of 6.25 contributes only 0.625 to Y under that SCM. Section 6 also defines regret with the opposite sign from the maximization formulation. These discrepancies must be reconciled with the implementation before the regret and robustness results can be verified.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the claimed framework release: the manuscript provides no repository link, and important details such as the outer UCB exploration coefficient, intervention bounds, and precise acquisition rule for the adapted CaBO baseline are insufficiently specified.
